---
title: "Write your first hook in under five minutes"
---

By the end, Claude Code stops your agent from finishing a UI change it never looked at, and you
have a second hook that proves itself with a passing test — `uvx capt-hook test` prints
`5 passed` and exits zero.

Before you begin, you need [uv installed](installation.qmd) and a project open in Claude Code.
Every command runs through `uvx`, so nothing else is installed.

## 1. Scaffold

```bash
uvx capt-hook init
```

`init` creates `.claude/hooks/`, wires Claude Code's settings, installs the
[helper skills](skills.qmd), and arms the [session reviewer](../guide/session-reviewer.qmd).
You're already live, with no separate wiring step. To drive setup from Claude instead, install
the plugin and ask it to "set up captain hook" — see [Agent Skills](skills.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip title="Checkpoint"}
`init` prints `Scaffolded .claude/hooks/example.py + .claude/settings.json.` and lists the five
events it wired (`PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`, `SubagentStop`, `SessionEnd`).
:::

## 2. Read your first hook

`init` dropped an example into `.claude/hooks/`. At its core is one declarative value built from
an action and two conditions.

<!-- gd-embed-fragment: canonical_hook -->

The action is `gate(...)`, which blocks the agent at `Stop` with the message you give it. The
`only_if` condition makes the gate fire only when the agent edited a file matching one of these
globs, while `skip_if` keeps the gate quiet if the agent already used `agent-browser` this
session. That's the whole model. An event, conditions that decide when it fires, and an action.

## 3. Watch it fire

Reload the project so Claude Code picks up the settings. Edit a file under `src/components/` and
try to end the turn. The gate blocks with your message, and the agent turns to `agent-browser`
to review the change before finishing.

## 4. Test your hooks

No git-hook tool can do this part, where every deterministic hook carries its own tests. Add a
second hook to `.claude/hooks/safety.py`:

```python
from captain_hook import Allow, Block, Input, block_command

block_command(
    ["git", "stash"],
    reason="Use jj instead",
    hint="Run `jj shelve`",
    tests={
        Input(command="git stash"): Block(),    # this command is blocked
        Input(command="git status"): Allow(),   # this one is fine
    },
)
```

Run the tests from your project root, where `--hooks` defaults to `.claude/hooks`. The scaffolded
`example.py` carries three cases of its own, so your two run alongside them:

```bash
uvx capt-hook test
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Checkpoint"}
```
  PASS  example:hook_699f6d38:Input(command='rm -rf /', tool='Bash')
  PASS  example:hook_699f6d38:Input(command='rm -rf build/', tool='Bash')
  PASS  example:hook_699f6d38:Input(command='rm notes.txt', tool='Bash')
  PASS  safety:hook_c10315f3:Input(command='git stash')
  PASS  safety:hook_c10315f3:Input(command='git status')

5 tests: 5 passed, 0 failed, 0 errors, 0 skipped
```
An import error instead means the hook file has a syntax problem — the traceback names the line.
:::

Each id is the hook file's stem plus a content hash, then the `Input` that produced the case.
Break an expectation and the line flips to `FAIL` and the command exits non-zero. Drop the same
check into CI and a regressed hook fails the build. LLM-backed hooks run their tests against a
stubbed verdict, so the whole suite stays deterministic.
